The question of who gave the first permission to the East India Company to trade has complementary answers depending on scope. Queen Elizabeth I issued a proclamation on 31st December 1600, granting the East India Company trading rights for fifteen years [d3]; British merchants founded the company in 1600 CE with her permission [d4]. This was the foundational charter that established the company itself [d1][d4]. Within India specifically, Sir Thomas Roe visited the court of Mughal Emperor Jahangir in 1615 CE and obtained permission to trade in Surat, after an earlier attempt by Captain William Hawkins in 1608 had failed due to Portuguese pressure [d4][d6]. Additionally, Mughal Emperor Farooq Siyara issued a Farmaan in 1717 allowing the East India Company to trade without tax in Bengal Province and Agra, a later and distinct permission [d7]. Thus, Queen Elizabeth I gave the first permission for the company's formation and trade broadly, while Jahangir gave the first permission to trade within India [d2][d4][d5].
